cards.front: State Tom Mitchell's formal definition of Machine Learning and illustrate with an example.
cards.back:
A computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P, if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E.
• Example (Spam Filter): Task T = classifying email as spam/not-spam; Experience E = watching user label emails; Performance measure P = fraction of emails correctly classified.
cards.formula_or_code: Learning = Experience E + Task T + Performance P

cards.front: Differentiate between Supervised, Unsupervised, Semi-Supervised, and Reinforcement Learning.
cards.back:
• Supervised: Trained on labeled data {(x_i, y_i)}. Tasks: Classification (discrete targets) and Regression (continuous targets).
• Unsupervised: Given unlabeled data {x_i} to find hidden patterns. Tasks: Clustering, Dimensionality Reduction (PCA), Density Estimation.
• Semi-Supervised: Combines a small set of labeled data with a large amount of inexpensive unlabeled data.
• Reinforcement Learning (RL): Agent learns optimal policy through trial-and-error by taking actions in an environment to maximize cumulative reward.
cards.formula_or_code: Supervised (Labels) | Unsupervised (Patterns) | RL (Rewards/MDP)

cards.front: How is Reinforcement Learning modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP)?
cards.back:
Modeled as 5-tuple (S, A, P, R, γ):
• S: Set of states
• A: Set of actions
• P(s' | s, a): Transition probability from state s to s' under action a
• R(s, a): Immediate reward received
• γ ∈ [0, 1): Discount factor
• Objective: Maximize expected cumulative discounted return: G_t = ∑_{k=0}^∞ γ^k · r_{t+k+1}
cards.formula_or_code: G_t = sum_{k=0}^inf gamma^k * r_{t+k+1}

cards.front: What is the principle behind Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) and why is log-likelihood used?
cards.back:
• Principle: Given i.i.d. data D = {x1..xN}, MLE selects parameter θ that maximizes probability of observing the data:
  L(θ; D) = ∏_{i=1}^N P(x_i | θ)
• Log-Likelihood: Natural log is strictly monotonically increasing, so maximizing L(θ) is equivalent to maximizing:
  ℓ(θ) = ln L(θ) = ∑_{i=1}^N ln P(x_i | θ)
• Why: Converts cumbersome products into sums, simplifies differentiation, and prevents floating-point numerical underflow.
cards.formula_or_code: theta_MLE = argmax_theta sum_{i=1}^N ln P(x_i | theta)

cards.front: State the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) objective and write its closed-form Normal Equation.
cards.back:
• Objective: In linear regression y = Xθ + ε, OLS minimizes the Sum of Squared Errors:
  J(θ) = ||y - Xθ||^2 = (y - Xθ)^T (y - Xθ)
• Normal Equation: Taking derivative ∇_θ J(θ) = 0 yields:
  X^T X θ = X^T y  ⇒  θ_OLS = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y
• Equivalence: When errors ε_i ~ N(0, σ^2) are Gaussian i.i.d., OLS is mathematically identical to MLE!
cards.formula_or_code: Normal Equation: theta = (X^T * X)^(-1) * X^T * y

cards.front: Compare Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) and Minimum Mean Square Estimation (MMSE).
cards.back:
• MAP (Mode of Posterior):
  θ_MAP = argmax_θ P(θ | D) = argmax_θ [ ln P(D | θ) + ln P(θ) ]
  Selects the single most probable parameter point. (Gaussian prior ≡ L2 Ridge; Laplace prior ≡ L1 Lasso).
• MMSE (Mean of Posterior):
  θ_MMSE = E[θ | D] = ∫ θ · P(θ | D) dθ
  Minimizes expected squared error E[(θ - θ_hat)^2]. Computes the center of mass of the posterior distribution.
cards.formula_or_code: MAP = Mode of Posterior | MMSE = Mean of Posterior E[theta | D]

cards.front: Compare Batch Gradient Descent (BGD), Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), and Mini-Batch GD.
cards.back:
• Batch GD: Computes gradient over ENTIRE dataset (size N) per step. Stable, smooth, slow for huge N, requires high memory.
• Stochastic GD (SGD): Updates weights for EACH single training sample. Extremely fast, lightweight, noisy path that helps escape local minima, but oscillates and never truly settles.
• Mini-Batch GD: Computes gradient over small batches (e.g. 32 to 256 samples). Balances smooth convergence with GPU matrix vectorization efficiency.
cards.formula_or_code: Update: theta := theta - eta * grad_J(theta)

cards.front: Why is Linear Regression unsuitable for classification, and how does Logistic Regression solve this?
cards.back:
• Linear Regression outputs unbounded values (-∞ to +∞), which cannot represent probabilities, and extreme outliers heavily distort linear decision boundaries.
• Logistic Regression applies the Sigmoid function to map any real output into probability range (0, 1):
  σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z))
• Decision: If P(y=1|x) = σ(θ^T x) ≥ 0.5 (i.e. θ^T x ≥ 0), predict class 1.
cards.formula_or_code: Sigmoid: sigma(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z) | Derivative: sigma(z)*(1 - sigma(z))

cards.front: Why is Mean Squared Error (MSE) NOT used as the loss function in Logistic Regression?
cards.back:
• When MSE is combined with the non-linear Sigmoid function, the resulting cost surface is NON-CONVEX with numerous local minima and flat plateau regions (vanishing gradients).
• Binary Cross-Entropy (Log-Loss) is used instead:
  J(θ) = - (1/N) ∑ [ y_i ln(y_hat_i) + (1 - y_i) ln(1 - y_hat_i) ]
• Cross-Entropy is strictly CONVEX, guaranteeing that Gradient Descent converges to the global minimum.
cards.formula_or_code: Log-Loss: J(theta) = -(1/N) * sum [y*ln(p) + (1-y)*ln(1-p)] (Strictly Convex)

cards.front: State the formulas for Shannon Entropy and Information Gain used in the ID3 Decision Tree algorithm.
cards.back:
• Shannon Entropy (Impurity of set S with c classes):
  H(S) = - ∑_{i=1}^c p_i · log2(p_i)
  (Pure set: H=0; Even binary split: H=1 bit).
• Information Gain (Expected reduction in entropy by splitting on attribute A):
  Gain(S, A) = H(S) - ∑_{v ∈ Values(A)} (|S_v| / |S|) · H(S_v)
• ID3 Criterion: Select the attribute that yields the MAXIMUM Information Gain as the split node.
cards.formula_or_code: H(S) = -sum p_i * log2(p_i) | Gain = H(S) - sum (|S_v|/|S|)*H(S_v)

cards.front: Define Gini Impurity used in CART and compare CART with ID3.
cards.back:
• Gini Impurity:
  Gini(S) = 1 - ∑_{i=1}^c p_i^2
  (Pure node: Gini = 0; Equal 2-class split: Gini = 1 - (0.5^2 + 0.5^2) = 0.5).
• ID3 vs CART:
  - ID3: Multi-way branch splits, uses Information Gain, categorical attributes only.
  - CART: Strictly BINARY splits, uses Gini Impurity (classification) or variance reduction (regression), handles both continuous and categorical data.
cards.formula_or_code: Gini(S) = 1 - sum p_i^2 | CART produces binary trees

cards.front: Differentiate between Pre-Pruning and Post-Pruning in Decision Trees.
cards.back:
• Pre-Pruning (Early Stopping): Halts tree expansion during construction if conditions are met (e.g. max depth reached, node sample count < min_samples_split, info gain < threshold). Fast, but risks stopping too early (horizon effect).
• Post-Pruning (Cost-Complexity Pruning): Grows full unconstrained tree first, then prunes subtrees upward using validation data by minimizing cost function C_α(T) = R(T) + α|T|. Produces superior generalization.
cards.formula_or_code: Cost-Complexity: C_alpha(T) = R(T) + alpha * |T|

cards.front: State the Bias-Variance Decomposition and explain Underfitting vs Overfitting.
cards.back:
Expected Test Error = Bias^2 + Variance + Irreducible Error (σ^2)
• Bias: Error introduced by overly simplistic model assumptions. High Bias ⇒ Underfitting (model fails to capture training patterns; high train & test error).
• Variance: Sensitivity of model to specific training set fluctuations. High Variance ⇒ Overfitting (model captures noise/outliers; low train error but high test error).
• Goal: Sweet spot minimizing total generalization error.
cards.formula_or_code: Total Error = Bias^2 + Variance + sigma^2

cards.front: Compare Ridge (L2) and Lasso (L1) Regularization and explain geometrically why Lasso creates sparse models.
cards.back:
• Ridge (L2): Adds penalty λ ∑ θ_j^2. Shrinks weights close to zero but NEVER exactly zero. Retains all features. Invertible even with multicollinearity: (X^T X + λI)^(-1) X^T y.
• Lasso (L1): Adds penalty λ ∑ |θ_j|. Drives unimportant weights strictly to EXACT ZERO. Performs automatic feature selection.
• Geometric Reason: The L1 constraint region is a diamond with sharp corners on axes (|θ1| + |θ2| ≤ t), while L2 is a smooth circle (θ1^2 + θ2^2 ≤ t). Contours of MSE loss typically intersect the L1 diamond at a corner where one coordinate is exactly 0!
cards.formula_or_code: Ridge: MSE + lambda * sum(theta_j^2) | Lasso: MSE + lambda * sum(|theta_j|)

cards.front: Differentiate between Lazy Learners and Eager Learners with examples.
cards.back:
• Lazy Learners (e.g. KNN, Case-Based Reasoning):
  - Training Phase: Zero / O(1) - simply stores training instances in memory.
  - Query Phase: Expensive O(N · d) - scans all points to compute distances.
  - Memory: Retains all training data.
• Eager Learners (e.g. Decision Trees, Logistic Regression, SVM):
  - Training Phase: Expensive - constructs explicit model / parameters.
  - Query Phase: Fast O(1) or O(depth) - evaluates learned function.
  - Memory: Training data can be discarded after model is built.
cards.formula_or_code: Lazy: O(1) train, O(N*d) query | Eager: O(N*d*epochs) train, O(1) query

cards.front: How does KNN work, what distance metrics are used, and what is the impact of hyperparameter K?
cards.back:
• Algorithm: Computes distance from query x_q to all stored points, picks K nearest neighbors, predicts class via majority vote (or mean for regression).
• Distance Metrics: Euclidean (L2: sqrt(sum(x-z)^2)), Manhattan (L1: sum|x-z|), Minkowski (Lp).
• Effect of K:
  - Small K (e.g. K=1): Complex jagged boundary, low bias, high variance (sensitive to noise/overfitting).
  - Large K (e.g. K=N): Overly smooth boundary, high bias, low variance (underfitting).
  - Optimal K: Chosen via cross-validation (odd number prevents voting ties).
cards.formula_or_code: Small K -> High Variance | Large K -> High Bias

cards.front: What is the Curse of Dimensionality in distance-based algorithms like KNN?
cards.back:
• As feature dimensions d increase, the volume of feature space grows exponentially (V ∝ r^d). Data points become extremely sparse.
• Pairwise distance phenomenon: In high dimensions, the distance between any two random points converges to approximately the same value (distance to nearest neighbor ≈ distance to farthest neighbor).
• Consequence: Distance metrics lose all discriminative power, degrading KNN accuracy unless dimensionality reduction (PCA, feature selection) is applied.
cards.formula_or_code: Volume grows as r^d -> Pairwise distances become equidistant

cards.front: State the Naive Bayes classification rule and explain the class-conditional independence assumption.
cards.back:
• Bayes' Theorem: P(C_k | X) = [ P(X | C_k) · P(C_k) ] / P(X)
• Naive Conditional Independence Assumption: Assumes all feature attributes x_1..x_d are conditionally independent given class C_k:
  P(x_1, x_2, ..., x_d | C_k) = ∏_{j=1}^d P(x_j | C_k)
• MAP Decision Rule:
  y_hat = argmax_{C_k} P(C_k) · ∏_{j=1}^d P(x_j | C_k)
  Computed in log-space: argmax [ ln P(C_k) + ∑ ln P(x_j | C_k) ].
cards.formula_or_code: y_hat = argmax_C P(C) * prod_{j=1}^d P(x_j | C)

cards.front: What is the Zero-Frequency problem in Naive Bayes and how does Laplace Smoothing fix it?
cards.back:
• Problem: If attribute value x_j never appeared with class C_k in training data, its conditional probability is P(x_j | C_k) = 0. Because Naive Bayes multiplies all probabilities, that single 0 wipes out the entire class probability product to ZERO!
• Solution (Laplace Add-1 Correction):
  Adds pseudocount 1 to numerator and |V| (number of unique attribute values) to denominator:
  P_Laplace(x_j = v | C_k) = [ count(x_j=v, C_k) + 1 ] / [ count(C_k) + |V| ]
  Guarantees strictly non-zero probabilities.
cards.formula_or_code: P(x_j | C) = [count(x_j, C) + 1] / [count(C) + |V|]

cards.front: Explain the Maximum Margin principle in SVM and define Support Vectors.
cards.back:
• Principle: Finds the optimal decision hyperplane w^T x + b = 0 that separates two classes with the MAXIMUM geometric margin.
• Bounding Canonical Planes: w^T x + b = +1 and w^T x + b = -1.
• Geometric Margin: Width = 2 / ||w||. Maximizing 2/||w|| is equivalent to minimizing (1/2)||w||^2.
• Support Vectors: The critical data points lying directly on the margins (y_i(w^T x_i + b) = 1). The decision boundary is determined SOLELY by support vectors; all other training points can be removed without altering the boundary!
cards.formula_or_code: Margin = 2 / ||w|| | Optimization: min (1/2)||w||^2 s.t. y_i(w^T x_i + b) >= 1

cards.front: How does Soft-Margin SVM handle non-separable data and outliers?
cards.back:
• Introduces non-negative Slack Variables ξ_i ≥ 0 that allow points to violate the margin:
  min_{w, b, ξ} (1/2)||w||^2 + C ∑_{i=1}^N ξ_i
  subject to: y_i(w^T x_i + b) ≥ 1 - ξ_i,  ξ_i ≥ 0
• Penalty Parameter C:
  - Large C: Strict penalty for violations ⇒ Narrow margin, low bias, high variance (overfitting risk).
  - Small C: Tolerant of violations ⇒ Wide margin, smoother boundary, high bias (underfitting risk).
• Hinge Loss: Loss = max(0, 1 - y_i · f(x_i)).
cards.formula_or_code: Objective: min (1/2)||w||^2 + C * sum(xi_i) | Hinge Loss: max(0, 1 - y*f(x))

cards.front: Define a Kernel Function and explain the significance of high vs low Gamma in an RBF Kernel.
cards.back:
• Kernel Function: Computes inner product in high-dimensional transformed space directly in input space without explicit coordinate transformation: K(x, z) = ⟨ϕ(x), ϕ(z)⟩.
• RBF / Gaussian Kernel: K(x, z) = exp(-γ ||x - z||^2) where γ = 1 / (2σ^2).
• Gamma (γ) Significance:
  - High γ: Small σ (narrow bell curve). Influence of each support vector is localized. Decision boundary is tight and complex around training points ⇒ High Variance / Severe Overfitting.
  - Low γ: Large σ (broad bell curve). Support vectors have wide global influence. Decision boundary becomes overly smooth ⇒ High Bias / Underfitting.
cards.formula_or_code:
RBF: K(x, z) = exp(-gamma * ||x - z||^2)
High gamma -> Overfitting | Low gamma -> Underfitting

cards.front: What is Ensemble Learning and how does Hard Voting differ from Soft Voting?
cards.back:
• Ensemble Learning combines multiple base models to produce a single meta-model with superior accuracy and generalization (grounded in Condorcet's Jury Theorem).
• Hard Voting (Majority): Predicts the class label receiving the most votes across models: y_hat = mode{h1(x), h2(x), ..., hM(x)}.
• Soft Voting (Probability Averaging): Averages predicted class probabilities across all models and selects the class with highest probability: y_hat = argmax_c (1/M) ∑ P_m(y=c|x). Gives higher weight to confident models.
cards.formula_or_code: Hard = Mode of classes | Soft = Argmax of average probabilities

cards.front: Explain Bootstrap Aggregation (Bagging) and Out-of-Bag (OOB) error estimation.
cards.back:
• Bagging (Breiman): Trains homogeneous base models independently in parallel on bootstrap samples (drawn with replacement of size N) to reduce VARIANCE without increasing bias.
• Out-of-Bag (OOB) Error:
  - Probability an instance is NOT chosen in N draws: (1 - 1/N)^N → 1/e ≈ 36.8%.
  - The remaining ~36.8% unpicked samples form the OOB set for that tree.
  - Evaluating each sample using only trees where it was OOB provides an unbiased test error estimate without a separate validation set!
cards.formula_or_code: Bootstrap: ~63.2% unique, ~36.8% OOB (lim (1 - 1/N)^N = 1/e)

cards.front: How does Random Forest improve upon standard Bagging of Decision Trees?
cards.back:
• In standard Bagging, if a few strong features exist, all trees split on them first, creating highly correlated trees with limited variance reduction.
• Random Forest introduces Feature Bagging (Random Subspace Method):
  At every split in each tree, it considers a random subset of m features (m = sqrt(d) for classification, d/3 for regression) rather than all d features.
• Effect: De-correlates the individual trees, drastically reducing ensemble variance while resisting overfitting.
cards.formula_or_code: Feature subset size at each split: m = sqrt(d)

cards.front: Compare Bagging vs Boosting and state the AdaBoost weight update rules.
cards.back:
• Bagging: Parallel, independent training, reduces Variance (e.g. Random Forest).
• Boosting: Sequential training where each learner focuses on errors of previous learners, reduces Bias (e.g. AdaBoost, XGBoost).
• AdaBoost Mechanics:
  1. Classifier weight: α_t = (1/2) · ln((1 - ε_t) / ε_t)
  2. Sample weights update: w_i := w_i · exp(-α_t · y_i · h_t(x_i)) / Z_t
     (Misclassified samples have weights multiplied by e^(α_t); correctly classified samples are downweighted).
  3. Final prediction: H(x) = sign(∑ α_t · h_t(x)).
cards.formula_or_code: alpha_t = (1/2)*ln((1 - eps)/eps) | w_i := w_i * exp(-alpha * y * h) / Z

cards.front: Explain Stacked Generalization (Stacking) and how Out-of-Fold cross-validation prevents data leakage.
cards.back:
• Stacking combines diverse HETEROGENEOUS base models (SVM, Random Forest, Logistic Regression) at Level-0, whose predictions serve as meta-features for a Level-1 Meta-Learner.
• Preventing Leakage via K-Fold OOF:
  Base models generate predictions on held-out validation folds (out-of-fold). The concatenated out-of-fold predictions form the training set for the Meta-Learner, ensuring it trains on realistic out-of-sample predictions.
cards.formula_or_code: Level 0: Heterogeneous models -> Level 1: Meta-Learner on OOF predictions

cards.front: Define Confusion Matrix components and write formulas for Accuracy, Precision, Recall, Specificity, and F1-Score.
cards.back:
• Matrix: TP (True Pos), FP (Type I error), FN (Type II error), TN (True Neg).
• Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN) [Misleading for imbalanced data!]
• Precision = TP / (TP + FP) [Purity of positive predictions]
• Recall (Sensitivity / TPR) = TP / (TP + FN) [Coverage of actual positives]
• Specificity (TNR) = TN / (TN + FP)
• F1-Score = 2 · (Precision · Recall) / (Precision + Recall) [Harmonic mean]
cards.formula_or_code: Precision = TP/(TP+FP) | Recall = TP/(TP+FN) | F1 = 2*P*R/(P+R)

cards.front: Explain the working principle of the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve and AUC.
cards.back:
• ROC Curve: Plots True Positive Rate (Recall/Sensitivity) on Y-axis vs False Positive Rate (FPR = 1 - Specificity = FP/(TN+FP)) on X-axis across all decision thresholds τ ∈ [0, 1].
• Key Points: (0,0) predicts all negative; (1,1) predicts all positive; Diagonal is random guessing; (0,1) is the perfect classifier.
• AUC (Area Under Curve): Measures area under ROC. Statistically equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive sample is ranked higher than a randomly chosen negative sample (AUC=1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is random).
cards.formula_or_code: ROC = Plot of TPR vs FPR | AUC = Probability of correct ranking

  (Pure node: Gini = 0; Equal 2-class split: Gini = 1 - (0.5^2 + 0.5^2) = 0.5).
• ID3 vs CART:
  - ID3: Multi-way branch splits, uses Information Gain, categorical attributes only.
  - CART: Strictly BINARY splits, uses Gini Impurity (classification) or variance reduction (regression), handles both continuous and categorical data.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Gini(S) = 1 - sum p_i^2 | CART produces binary trees

flashcards.front: Differentiate between Pre-Pruning and Post-Pruning in Decision Trees.
flashcards.back:
• Pre-Pruning (Early Stopping): Halts tree expansion during construction if conditions are met (e.g. max depth reached, node sample count < min_samples_split, info gain < threshold). Fast, but risks stopping too early (horizon effect).
• Post-Pruning (Cost-Complexity Pruning): Grows full unconstrained tree first, then prunes subtrees upward using validation data by minimizing cost function C_α(T) = R(T) + α|T|. Produces superior generalization.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Cost-Complexity: C_alpha(T) = R(T) + alpha * |T|

flashcards.front: State the Bias-Variance Decomposition and explain Underfitting vs Overfitting.
flashcards.back:
Expected Test Error = Bias^2 + Variance + Irreducible Error (σ^2)
• Bias: Error introduced by overly simplistic model assumptions. High Bias ⇒ Underfitting (model fails to capture training patterns; high train & test error).
• Variance: Sensitivity of model to specific training set fluctuations. High Variance ⇒ Overfitting (model captures noise/outliers; low train error but high test error).
• Goal: Sweet spot minimizing total generalization error.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Total Error = Bias^2 + Variance + sigma^2

flashcards.front: Compare Ridge (L2) and Lasso (L1) Regularization and explain geometrically why Lasso creates sparse models.
flashcards.back:
• Ridge (L2): Adds penalty λ ∑ θ_j^2. Shrinks weights close to zero but NEVER exactly zero. Retains all features. Invertible even with multicollinearity: (X^T X + λI)^(-1) X^T y.
• Lasso (L1): Adds penalty λ ∑ |θ_j|. Drives unimportant weights strictly to EXACT ZERO. Performs automatic feature selection.
• Geometric Reason: The L1 constraint region is a diamond with sharp corners on axes (|θ1| + |θ2| ≤ t), while L2 is a smooth circle (θ1^2 + θ2^2 ≤ t). Contours of MSE loss typically intersect the L1 diamond at a corner where one coordinate is exactly 0!
flashcards.formula_or_code: Ridge: MSE + lambda * sum(theta_j^2) | Lasso: MSE + lambda * sum(|theta_j|)

flashcards.front: Differentiate between Lazy Learners and Eager Learners with examples.
flashcards.back:
• Lazy Learners (e.g. KNN, Case-Based Reasoning):
  - Training Phase: Zero / O(1) - simply stores training instances in memory.
  - Query Phase: Expensive O(N · d) - scans all points to compute distances.
  - Memory: Retains all training data.
• Eager Learners (e.g. Decision Trees, Logistic Regression, SVM):
  - Training Phase: Expensive - constructs explicit model / parameters.
  - Query Phase: Fast O(1) or O(depth) - evaluates learned function.
  - Memory: Training data can be discarded after model is built.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Lazy: O(1) train, O(N*d) query | Eager: O(N*d*epochs) train, O(1) query

flashcards.front: How does KNN work, what distance metrics are used, and what is the impact of hyperparameter K?
flashcards.back:
• Algorithm: Computes distance from query x_q to all stored points, picks K nearest neighbors, predicts class via majority vote (or mean for regression).
• Distance Metrics: Euclidean (L2: sqrt(sum(x-z)^2)), Manhattan (L1: sum|x-z|), Minkowski (Lp).
• Effect of K:
  - Small K (e.g. K=1): Complex jagged boundary, low bias, high variance (sensitive to noise/overfitting).
  - Large K (e.g. K=N): Overly smooth boundary, high bias, low variance (underfitting).
  - Optimal K: Chosen via cross-validation (odd number prevents voting ties).
flashcards.formula_or_code: Small K -> High Variance | Large K -> High Bias

flashcards.front: What is the Curse of Dimensionality in distance-based algorithms like KNN?
flashcards.back:
• As feature dimensions d increase, the volume of feature space grows exponentially (V ∝ r^d). Data points become extremely sparse.
• Pairwise distance phenomenon: In high dimensions, the distance between any two random points converges to approximately the same value (distance to nearest neighbor ≈ distance to farthest neighbor).
• Consequence: Distance metrics lose all discriminative power, degrading KNN accuracy unless dimensionality reduction (PCA, feature selection) is applied.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Volume grows as r^d -> Pairwise distances become equidistant

flashcards.front: State the Naive Bayes classification rule and explain the class-conditional independence assumption.
flashcards.back:
• Bayes' Theorem: P(C_k | X) = [ P(X | C_k) · P(C_k) ] / P(X)
• Naive Conditional Independence Assumption: Assumes all feature attributes x_1..x_d are conditionally independent given class C_k:
  P(x_1, x_2, ..., x_d | C_k) = ∏_{j=1}^d P(x_j | C_k)
• MAP Decision Rule:
  y_hat = argmax_{C_k} P(C_k) · ∏_{j=1}^d P(x_j | C_k)
  Computed in log-space: argmax [ ln P(C_k) + ∑ ln P(x_j | C_k) ].
flashcards.formula_or_code: y_hat = argmax_C P(C) * prod_{j=1}^d P(x_j | C)

flashcards.front: What is the Zero-Frequency problem in Naive Bayes and how does Laplace Smoothing fix it?
flashcards.back:
• Problem: If attribute value x_j never appeared with class C_k in training data, its conditional probability is P(x_j | C_k) = 0. Because Naive Bayes multiplies all probabilities, that single 0 wipes out the entire class probability product to ZERO!
• Solution (Laplace Add-1 Correction):
  Adds pseudocount 1 to numerator and |V| (number of unique attribute values) to denominator:
  P_Laplace(x_j = v | C_k) = [ count(x_j=v, C_k) + 1 ] / [ count(C_k) + |V| ]
  Guarantees strictly non-zero probabilities.
flashcards.formula_or_code: P(x_j | C) = [count(x_j, C) + 1] / [count(C) + |V|]

flashcards.front: Explain the Maximum Margin principle in SVM and define Support Vectors.
flashcards.back:
• Principle: Finds the optimal decision hyperplane w^T x + b = 0 that separates two classes with the MAXIMUM geometric margin.
• Bounding Canonical Planes: w^T x + b = +1 and w^T x + b = -1.
• Geometric Margin: Width = 2 / ||w||. Maximizing 2/||w|| is equivalent to minimizing (1/2)||w||^2.
• Support Vectors: The critical data points lying directly on the margins (y_i(w^T x_i + b) = 1). The decision boundary is determined SOLELY by support vectors; all other training points can be removed without altering the boundary!
flashcards.formula_or_code: Margin = 2 / ||w|| | Optimization: min (1/2)||w||^2 s.t. y_i(w^T x_i + b) >= 1

flashcards.front: How does Soft-Margin SVM handle non-separable data and outliers?
flashcards.back:
• Introduces non-negative Slack Variables ξ_i ≥ 0 that allow points to violate the margin:
  min_{w, b, ξ} (1/2)||w||^2 + C ∑_{i=1}^N ξ_i
  subject to: y_i(w^T x_i + b) ≥ 1 - ξ_i,  ξ_i ≥ 0
• Penalty Parameter C:
  - Large C: Strict penalty for violations ⇒ Narrow margin, low bias, high variance (overfitting risk).
  - Small C: Tolerant of violations ⇒ Wide margin, smoother boundary, high bias (underfitting risk).
• Hinge Loss: Loss = max(0, 1 - y_i · f(x_i)).
flashcards.formula_or_code: Objective: min (1/2)||w||^2 + C * sum(xi_i) | Hinge Loss: max(0, 1 - y*f(x))

flashcards.front: Define a Kernel Function and explain the significance of high vs low Gamma in an RBF Kernel.
flashcards.back:
• Kernel Function: Computes inner product in high-dimensional transformed space directly in input space without explicit coordinate transformation: K(x, z) = ⟨ϕ(x), ϕ(z)⟩.
• RBF / Gaussian Kernel: K(x, z) = exp(-γ ||x - z||^2) where γ = 1 / (2σ^2).
• Gamma (γ) Significance:
  - High γ: Small σ (narrow bell curve). Influence of each support vector is localized. Decision boundary is tight and complex around training points ⇒ High Variance / Severe Overfitting.
  - Low γ: Large σ (broad bell curve). Support vectors have wide global influence. Decision boundary becomes overly smooth ⇒ High Bias / Underfitting.
flashcards.formula_or_code:
RBF: K(x, z) = exp(-gamma * ||x - z||^2)
High gamma -> Overfitting | Low gamma -> Underfitting

flashcards.front: What is Ensemble Learning and how does Hard Voting differ from Soft Voting?
flashcards.back:
• Ensemble Learning combines multiple base models to produce a single meta-model with superior accuracy and generalization (grounded in Condorcet's Jury Theorem).
• Hard Voting (Majority): Predicts the class label receiving the most votes across models: y_hat = mode{h1(x), h2(x), ..., hM(x)}.
• Soft Voting (Probability Averaging): Averages predicted class probabilities across all models and selects the class with highest probability: y_hat = argmax_c (1/M) ∑ P_m(y=c|x). Gives higher weight to confident models.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Hard = Mode of classes | Soft = Argmax of average probabilities

flashcards.front: Explain Bootstrap Aggregation (Bagging) and Out-of-Bag (OOB) error estimation.
flashcards.back:
• Bagging (Breiman): Trains homogeneous base models independently in parallel on bootstrap samples (drawn with replacement of size N) to reduce VARIANCE without increasing bias.
• Out-of-Bag (OOB) Error:
  - Probability an instance is NOT chosen in N draws: (1 - 1/N)^N → 1/e ≈ 36.8%.
  - The remaining ~36.8% unpicked samples form the OOB set for that tree.
  - Evaluating each sample using only trees where it was OOB provides an unbiased test error estimate without a separate validation set!
flashcards.formula_or_code: Bootstrap: ~63.2% unique, ~36.8% OOB (lim (1 - 1/N)^N = 1/e)

flashcards.front: How does Random Forest improve upon standard Bagging of Decision Trees?
flashcards.back:
• In standard Bagging, if a few strong features exist, all trees split on them first, creating highly correlated trees with limited variance reduction.
• Random Forest introduces Feature Bagging (Random Subspace Method):
  At every split in each tree, it considers a random subset of m features (m = sqrt(d) for classification, d/3 for regression) rather than all d features.
• Effect: De-correlates the individual trees, drastically reducing ensemble variance while resisting overfitting.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Feature subset size at each split: m = sqrt(d)

flashcards.front: Compare Bagging vs Boosting and state the AdaBoost weight update rules.
flashcards.back:
• Bagging: Parallel, independent training, reduces Variance (e.g. Random Forest).
• Boosting: Sequential training where each learner focuses on errors of previous learners, reduces Bias (e.g. AdaBoost, XGBoost).
• AdaBoost Mechanics:
  1. Classifier weight: α_t = (1/2) · ln((1 - ε_t) / ε_t)
  2. Sample weights update: w_i := w_i · exp(-α_t · y_i · h_t(x_i)) / Z_t
     (Misclassified samples have weights multiplied by e^(α_t); correctly classified samples are downweighted).
  3. Final prediction: H(x) = sign(∑ α_t · h_t(x)).
flashcards.formula_or_code: alpha_t = (1/2)*ln((1 - eps)/eps) | w_i := w_i * exp(-alpha * y * h) / Z

flashcards.front: Explain Stacked Generalization (Stacking) and how Out-of-Fold cross-validation prevents data leakage.
flashcards.back:
• Stacking combines diverse HETEROGENEOUS base models (SVM, Random Forest, Logistic Regression) at Level-0, whose predictions serve as meta-features for a Level-1 Meta-Learner.
• Preventing Leakage via K-Fold OOF:
  Base models generate predictions on held-out validation folds (out-of-fold). The concatenated out-of-fold predictions form the training set for the Meta-Learner, ensuring it trains on realistic out-of-sample predictions.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Level 0: Heterogeneous models -> Level 1: Meta-Learner on OOF predictions

flashcards.front: Define Confusion Matrix components and write formulas for Accuracy, Precision, Recall, Specificity, and F1-Score.
flashcards.back:
• Matrix: TP (True Pos), FP (Type I error), FN (Type II error), TN (True Neg).
• Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN) [Misleading for imbalanced data!]
• Precision = TP / (TP + FP) [Purity of positive predictions]
• Recall (Sensitivity / TPR) = TP / (TP + FN) [Coverage of actual positives]
• Specificity (TNR) = TN / (TN + FP)
• F1-Score = 2 · (Precision · Recall) / (Precision + Recall) [Harmonic mean]
flashcards.formula_or_code: Precision = TP/(TP+FP) | Recall = TP/(TP+FN) | F1 = 2*P*R/(P+R)

flashcards.front: Explain the working principle of the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve and AUC.
flashcards.back:
• ROC Curve: Plots True Positive Rate (Recall/Sensitivity) on Y-axis vs False Positive Rate (FPR = 1 - Specificity = FP/(TN+FP)) on X-axis across all decision thresholds τ ∈ [0, 1].
• Key Points: (0,0) predicts all negative; (1,1) predicts all positive; Diagonal is random guessing; (0,1) is the perfect classifier.
• AUC (Area Under Curve): Measures area under ROC. Statistically equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive sample is ranked higher than a randomly chosen negative sample (AUC=1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is random).
flashcards.formula_or_code: ROC = Plot of TPR vs FPR | AUC = Probability of correct ranking
